claims.note: Headline and description restate only figures this article recomputes from s3's printed CPU rows and s4's 600 s default; both strings equal the schema partial byte-for-byte.
Frames the reader's question as arithmetic over a measured rate and a turn count; no performance figure is asserted in this paragraph beyond referencing the benchmark rows.

pp and tg are quoted from llama-bench's own flag list; the comparative figures are that README's printed CPU rows for llama 7B mostly Q4_0 (1 thread pp 6.17 vs tg 4.05, 32 threads pp 59.00 vs 16.41), matched verbatim in this run. The paragraph states ratios and makes no order-of-magnitude claim; it also flags that the ratio depends on host and batch size.

Table rows are the corrected field semantics: prompt_eval_count is the total input prompt (cached plus newly evaluated) and prompt_eval_cached_count the cached subset, both matching s1's field descriptions; s5 assigns PromptEvalCount = CacheN + PromptN and PromptEvalCachedCount = CacheN; s6 derives the prompt eval rate as (PromptEvalCount - cached)/PromptEvalDuration, which is the table's prefill formula. The block asserts no measured number.

Quotes s6's rate printer (uncached := max(0, m.PromptEvalCount-cached), then uncached/duration) and s5's assignment of PromptMS to PromptEvalDuration; s1 shows prompt_eval_cached_count is an optional response field, so treating a missing value as 0 is the no-cache case the shipped rates() implements (pinned by the new unit tests). This replaces the round-3 claim that prompt_eval_count was the uncached count.
Inputs 6.17 and 4.05 tok/s are llama-bench README printed rows (7B Q4_0, CPU, 1 thread, pp 64, tg 16), labelled upstream sample output and not a measurement of this project or the reader's host.

512/6.17=82.98, 256/4.05=63.21, plus the declared 2 s overhead = 148.19 s; shares are 82.98/148.19 and 63.21/148.19 rounded to whole percent. Unchanged by the round-4 correction; reproduced by turn_budget.py example.
148.192 s times 10, 30 and 50 turns, converted to hours; identical inputs to the turn table above.
1024/6.17+63.21+2=231.17 s and 4096/6.17+63.21+2=729.07 s hold decode and overhead fixed; the 580.9 s delta is 663.86 minus 82.98 of prefill.

256/(600-82.98-2)=0.497 tok/s; the 600 s DEFAULT_TIMEOUT and DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES=2 were re-fetched verbatim this run from s4 (548 bytes, sha256 3f695647...), so 3 attempts x 148.19 s = 444.6 s. The paragraph's only change since the receipt was the repaired s4 link target.
6.17*600=3702 prompt tokens is the prefill-only ceiling; 4096 prompt tokens gives 663.86 s of prefill (729.07 s turn) and 8192 gives 1327.7 s, both past the 600 s default.
Ranking follows the worked example's own shares; 128 output tokens gives 31.60 s of decode and 116.59 s per turn at the same 512-token prompt and 2 s overhead.
Command block reproduces the shipped harness interface verbatim: measure, summarise and compute subcommands with the fixture and JSONL path arguments.

Describes what the shipped script now does: prefill numerator is prompt_eval_count minus prompt_eval_cached_count over the uncached-only duration, one fsync per record, and a 10 percent spread gate that reports rejected_noisy instead of medians. Verified by reading turn_budget.py in this tree and by the recorded test run.

Four tests added for the cache case: 64 tokens with 32 cached must yield 8.0 tok/s, a missing cached count must be treated as 0, a fully cached prompt must raise, and legacy records without the new fields must still resolve their prompt tokens.
